entities.label: Text
entities.summary:
The Romance of the Three Kingdoms, completed in the 14th century, is a monumental work of Chinese literature attributed to Luo Guanzhong. Set against the tumultuous backdrop of the late Eastern Han dynasty and the Three Kingdoms period (c. 184–280 CE), this historical novel intricately weaves facts and fiction, providing a vivid narrative that has significantly shaped Chinese cultural identity and historical consciousness. Key figures include the warlords Cao Cao, Liu Bei, and Sun Quan, whose exploits during this fragmented era are dramatized in the text, illustrating themes of loyalty, strategy, and the moral dilemmas of leadership.

The novel chronicles the power struggles and alliances formed among the three kingdoms—Wei, Shu, and Wu—after the fall of the Eastern Han dynasty. It is rich with historical events, such as the Battle of Red Cliffs in 208 CE, where a coalition of southern warlords defeated Cao Cao's forces. The text is not only a tale of military conflict; it also delves into the intricacies of political intrigue, emphasizing the importance of wisdom and virtue in governance. As a result, it has influenced both historical understanding and contemporary interpretations of this pivotal period in Chinese history.

The legacy of The Romance of the Three Kingdoms extends beyond literature; it has permeated various aspects of East Asian culture, inspiring operas, films, and video games, thereby ensuring its relevance across generations. The novel has also contributed to a nuanced understanding of Chinese history, prompting scholars to explore its complex characters and moral lessons. As historian H. A. Giles remarked, 'In this book, the past becomes not merely a record of events but a reflection of human nature itself.'

Today, it serves as a cultural touchstone, with its proverbs and characters entering the everyday lexicon of Chinese-speaking societies, illustrating the enduring impact of Luo Guanzhong's narrative artistry on Asian literature and identity.
